source.title: ADGraph: Accurate, Distributed Training on Large Graphs
source.authors: Lizhi Zhang; Zhi-Quan Lai; Feng Liu; Zhejiang Ran

record.tranche_reason: Tests batch-size effects and learning-rate scaling in distributed graph neural network training, a new setting for V5.
record.gate_note: The authors describe their results as test accuracy and connect large-batch training with generalization error. Tables 4–7 report separate test-accuracy results. The text does not report training accuracy alongside those results, so the training–test gap itself cannot be calculated. Cited results from prior work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Tests V5 in a new setting: graph node classification with distributed GraphSage and GAT, using a default 30-epoch budget. Reports test accuracy across batch sizes and GPU counts and compares fixed with scaled learning rates. GPU-count comparisons also change graph partitioning, so they do not isolate batch size alone.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: appropriately reducing per-GPU batch size and scaling the learning rate improve distributed GNN accuracy, allowing 32-GPU results comparable to single-GPU training. The authors also report 24–29-fold speedup.
record.recipe_differences: Distributed GraphSage and GAT node classification on large graph datasets; varies per-GPU batchsize and compares fixed with linearly scaled learning rates. It does not reproduce the original image or language benchmark recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Test accuracy changes with batchsize per GPU, GPU count, dataset, model, and learning-rate scaling. The paper holds training to 30 epochs in its default experiment settings.
record.problems: No training-accuracy values accompany the test-accuracy tables, so the training–test gap is not directly measured. No uncertainty estimates are reported. Batch-size and GPU-count comparisons vary together in Tables 4–5.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 4 and 5 report all six batchsize values across six GPU counts for each dataset, but only the 1-GPU and 32-GPU comparisons are extracted here to fit the 60-row limit. Omitted intermediate GPU-count entries are in Tables 4 and 5. Rows for GAT in Tables 4–5 are also omitted; the version-priority rule is satisfied by GraphSage results and the distinct model comparison in Tables 6–7.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting versus natural-label held-out performance.
Width sweeps beyond the width needed for interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning budgets.

Image and language workloads; longer training; warmup; normalization and regularization adaptations. Training performance is not reported alongside the test-accuracy comparisons, so optimization failure cannot be separated from a larger training–test gap.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its correlation with generalization gaps.
Removal of memorized examples versus random removal.

record.verdict_notes: The 30-epoch budget is stated in Table 2, so fixed-epoch comparisons should not be listed as untested. Near-equality at batch 250 and failure at extremely small batches do not qualify V5, which already specifies a workload-dependent threshold. Tables 4–5 do not explicitly identify their learning-rate settings; their batch-250 results coincide with the scaled-rate results in Tables 6–7. No uncertainty is reported. The record incorrectly says GAT rows were omitted from Tables 4–5: those tables contain only GraphSage results. Missing training accuracy limits mechanism attribution but does not prevent testing V5's held-out-performance prediction.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.

Image-classification and language benchmarks; training and test error together; epoch-budget comparisons to small-batch training; longer training, warmup, and normalization or regularization adaptations.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other generalization measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.

relationships.condition: GraphSage on 32 GPUs, comparing per-GPU batches 500 and 1000 with 250, under the default 30-epoch budget
relationships.reason: R8/R10/R12 show ogbn-products accuracy falling from 79.13% to 74.52%/72.8%; R20/R22/R24 show Reddit falling from 96.55% to 93.34%/92.39%.
relationships.display_finding: The study's results suggest larger per-GPU batches reduced GraphSage accuracy on both graph datasets. These results have not been verified.

relationships.condition: GraphSage and GAT, fixed learning rates, global batch increasing from 250 on one GPU to 8000 on 32 GPUs
relationships.reason: R25–R26, R28–R29, R31–R32 and R34–R35 show accuracy losses of 4.62, 2.12, 1.52 and 3.07 percentage points, respectively, although partitioning also changes.
relationships.display_finding: The study's results suggest lower accuracy as global batches increased, although graph partitioning also changed. These results have not been verified.

relationships.condition: GraphSage and GAT on both datasets, 32 GPUs with linearly scaled learning rates
relationships.reason: R27/R30/R33/R36 improve over the fixed-rate controls and approximately recover or exceed single-GPU accuracy, supporting V5's recipe-adaptation clause.
relationships.display_finding: The study's results suggest linear learning-rate scaling approximately recovered or exceeded single-GPU accuracy. These results have not been verified.
